title: The Siren Song of Marxism
author: Jeannette DeCelles-Zwerneman
summary: Jeannette DeCelles-Zwerneman, a veteran classical humanities teacher at Cana Academy, argues that classical schools have a curricular responsibility to inoculate students against the renewed appeal of Marxist ideology. She opens with the euphoria of the Berlin Wall's fall and Fukuyama's 'end of history,' then contrasts it with a 2025 Cato-YouGov poll showing 62% of Americans aged 18 to 29 view socialism favorably and 34% favor communism. She attributes this to teachers and professors who romanticize socialism, a Howard Zinn-influenced framing of American history, and very low historical literacy on NAEP. Her prescription has three parts: sustained, fair American history instruction across elementary and secondary school; a serious senior-year treatment of communism's record, including the Soviet Union, Mao's China, Tiananmen, and the Uyghurs, taught through dissident works such as Solzhenitsyn, Sharansky, and The Lives of Others; and an economics course built on Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics. She frames this as consistent with classical education's liberal commitment to intellectual freedom.
points: The author cites a March 2025 Cato-YouGov poll in which 62% of 18- to 29-year-olds viewed socialism favorably and 34% favored communism.
She argues historical illiteracy, with NAEP scores in the 13-17% range, is both the cause of this drift and the ground on which schools can respond.
American history should be a continuing, fair-minded inquiry across elementary and secondary grades rather than a one- or two-semester course.
A senior-year unit on communism's human toll, taught through dissident memoir and fiction like Solzhenitsyn and Sharansky, is proposed as preparation before college.
Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics is recommended for teaching incentives and outcomes as the basis of financial and economic literacy.
quotes: In 1992 Francis Fukuyama published his bestseller, The End of History and the Last Man, celebrating what he thought was the historical triumph of liberal democratic principles over all other forms of political order. Times were heady, and many believed that the Marxist ideology that fueled the Soviet Union and other communist states had been demonstrably proven wrong and could be dispensed with on “the ash heap of history.” The hope was that communism across the world would wither, die away, and be forgotten forever.

In a poll from March 2025, conducted by the Cato Institute and YouGov, 62% of Americans aged 18-29 viewed socialism favorably; a shocking 34% of that same age group favored communism explicitly. What accounts for the enduring allure of Marxist ideology despite its empirically proven failures?

Historically, enthusiasm for socialist-communist ideology fades once students leave college, begin working, get married, and have children since these achievements tend to temper youthful fantasies filled with fuzzy promises. What happens, however, if this latest generation fails to join the adult world of responsibility, work, and family and continues to harbor the empty promises of Marxist ideology?

This coursework cannot be managed in simply one or two semesters. It needs to be a continuing inquiry across elementary and secondary school, and it needs to be fair and truthful in its treatment of the country’s achievements and failures.

As Solzhenitsyn wrote in his forward to the abridged edition of his Gulag Archipelago, If it were possible for any nation to fathom another people’s bitter experience through a book, how much easier its future fate would become and how many calamities and mistakes it could avoid. But it is very difficult. There always is this fallacious belief: “It would not be the same here; here such things are impossible” (xxix).

This current cohort’s ignorance of this history fuels their absurd claims about the efficacy and righteousness of communism. A serious treatment of communism’s history must be undertaken in high school, preferably during senior year before the students land in college completely ill-equipped to resist the siren song of their professors. Especially helpful on this score is reading memoirs and fiction by dissidents who survived.

Finally, schools should introduce a serious economics course that imparts financial literacy to the students. Thomas Sowell’s Basic Economics: A Common Sense Guide to the Economy is an excellent beginning. This is not a typical economics textbook full of dreary graphs and pie charts. Sowell is a masterful storyteller and surveys various economic policies and their observable fruits, focusing on incentives and results rather than dreamy declarations of hoped-for expectations.

The recent surge of Marxist ideology should concern everyone in the classical education movement. Our mode of education is liberal and specifically devoted to the students’ intellectual freedom. Studying history and economics provides a powerful antidote to much of this confusion, and classical schools should shoulder their educational responsibilities on this score.
